opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's one of the more profound shifts in how search works. The core idea is that you move away from relying purely on the exact words someone typed and toward representing the *meaning* of the query and the meaning of the documents.

Early search was very lexical. If you typed a certain word, you'd find pages that contained that word, and then you'd layer on a lot of clever signals about link structure and quality. That works surprisingly well, but it's brittle. People phrase the same need in lots of different ways, and the page that best answers your question might not use any of your words.

Once you have learned representations, where a query and a document each map into a space where nearness means "these are about the same thing," you can match on topic and intent rather than surface form. Something like "how do I fix a bike chain that keeps slipping" can connect to a page about derailleur adjustment even if the vocabulary barely overlaps. That's a big deal for the long tail. A meaningful fraction of the queries we see every day are ones we've never seen before, and those are exactly the cases where you can't rely on memorized patterns. You need something that generalizes.

The other piece is that language models understand the query itself much better. Small words like "to," "for," and "not" can completely change what someone is asking, and older systems tended to treat them as noise. Models that read the whole query in context get those nuances right much more often.

Then there's the retrieval architecture. You can't run a huge model over billions of documents for every query, so in practice you have a cascade. You use relatively cheap learned embeddings to pull candidates out of an enormous index, and then you apply more and more expensive models to rerank a smaller and smaller set. The interesting engineering is in balancing quality against latency and compute at each stage.

More recently, the bigger shift is that the model isn't only helping you *find* the right pages. It can also help *synthesize* across them: pull together information from several sources, answer the question more directly, and still point you to where it came from so you can dig deeper. Grounding is really important there. You want the fluency and understanding of the model, but you want it anchored in actual documents so it's factual and attributable.

So I'd say representations improved search in layers. First better matching, then better understanding of queries, and now a much richer way of helping people get to what they actually wanted to know.

r001.rationale: The response says learned representations match topic and intent rather than surface wording, allowing a relevant page to match even when it does not use the query’s words.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I've thought about for a long time, actually going back well before the current wave of large language models. If you think about how search worked for most of its history, it was fundamentally about matching words. You typed in a query, we looked for documents that contained those words, and then we used a lot of signals, links, click behavior, hundreds of other things, to rank those documents. And that works surprisingly well, but it has a pretty fundamental limitation, which is that it doesn't really understand what you mean. It understands what you typed.

The thing that language-model-based representations give you is a way to get past that. Instead of representing a query as a bag of words, you represent it as a point in some high-dimensional space, and you represent documents, or passages, or images, or whatever, in that same space. And the model has learned, from enormous amounts of text, that "how do I fix a leaky tap" and "dripping faucet repair" should land close to each other even though they share basically no words. That's the kind of thing that used to require years of painstaking synonym engineering, and now it just falls out of the representation.

We started seeing this concretely with things like RankBrain, which was one of the first places we put a learned, embedding-style component into the ranking stack, and then BERT was a big step because it was bidirectional and actually attended to context. The canonical example people used to cite was a query like "can you get medicine for someone pharmacy," where the word "for" completely changes the meaning, and older systems would just throw it away as a stop word. A model that understands language keeps that nuance. MUM pushed it further toward multimodal and multilingual, so a representation learned from English content can help answer a query in a language where we have much less data.

The other thing I'd emphasize is that this is really about representations at every stage, not just the final ranking. Retrieval itself can be done with dense representations, so you're not limited to documents that happen to share vocabulary with the query. You can represent a document at the level of a passage rather than a whole page, which matters a lot for long documents where the answer is in paragraph fourteen. And once you have good representations, you can start doing things that look more like reasoning, where you decompose a complex information need into pieces and pull in evidence from multiple sources.

I'd be honest that there are real engineering challenges. Latency is a big one. You're serving an enormous number of queries and you can't spend a second of neural network compute on each one, so a lot of the work is in distillation, quantization, clever hardware like TPUs, and figuring out which parts of the stack actually need the big model versus a much smaller one. And there's the question of grounding, making sure that what the model represents is anchored to real, high-quality sources rather than just what sounds plausible. I think the combination of a model that understands language with a retrieval system that has a very good index of what's actually on the web is a much stronger thing than either alone, and that's really where I see the direction going.

r001.rationale: The response says learned representations place semantically similar queries and documents close together even when they share few or no words, allowing retrieval without exact word overlap.

astra-6.text:
I think one of the biggest benefits is that you can get beyond matching the words in a query to the words in a document. People often express what they’re looking for differently from the way an author expresses the answer. A language-model-based representation can help connect those two things.

For example, you might describe a problem without knowing the technical term for it. Ideally, Search should understand enough of what you mean to find a useful page even if that page uses quite different vocabulary. And context matters: the same word can mean different things depending on the rest of the query.

These representations can help both with finding candidate documents and with deciding which ones actually address your question. But understanding relevance is still only part of the problem. You also want the information to be reliable and current. So I think of language models as a powerful way to improve the understanding layer of Search, alongside the other signals that make a search result useful.

r001.rationale: The response says these representations can connect a query to a page using quite different vocabulary, without relying on the query’s exact words appearing in the page.

sol-6.1.text:
A big part of search is understanding what someone means, and that isn’t always captured by the exact words they type. People might describe something without knowing the terminology, and a really useful page might use completely different words. Language models give us representations that can bring those two things closer together.

They’re also better at using context. A word can mean very different things depending on the rest of the query, and small words can substantially change what someone is asking. So instead of treating a query as a collection of terms, you can get a richer representation of the question and compare that with a richer representation of a passage in a document.

That helps you retrieve and rank material that actually addresses the user’s intent. Of course, understanding relevance is only one part of search. You still need fresh information, reliable sources, and systems that can do all of this efficiently.

r001.rationale: The response says a useful page may use completely different words from the query and explains that language-model representations help connect them for retrieval.
